title: Minimum-Link Path in 2D
exact_target:
Can an exact path using the fewest straight segments around planar
polygonal obstacles be found in less than quadratic time?
definition_tex:
\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
Let $\mathcal O$ be pairwise interior-disjoint polygonal obstacles in
$\mathbb R^2$ with $n$ vertices in total, and let $s,t$ belong to the
same component of the free space
$F=\mathbb R^2\setminus\bigcup_{O\in\mathcal O}\operatorname{int}(O)$.
A feasible polygonal path consists of consecutive straight segments
joining $s$ to $t$, with its whole image in $F$. Boundary contact is
allowed. Merge consecutive collinear segments with no change of
direction before counting links.

The link distance is
\[
 \ell_F(s,t)=\min\{k: \text{a feasible }s\text{--}t\text{ path has }k
                         \text{ straight links}\}.
\]
Can this value and an attaining path be computed in subquadratic time
in $n$ in the standard real-arithmetic geometric model? Here
subquadratic means $o(n^2)$; a bound $O(n^{2-\delta})$ for some fixed
$\delta>0$ is a stronger target.

Link minimization counts changes of direction, not Euclidean path
length. The link directions are unrestricted, and obstacles may create
holes in the free-space domain. Results for simple polygons without
holes, rectilinear links, or approximate link counts do not by themselves
answer this formulation.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Can an exact path using the fewest straight segments around planar
polygonal obstacles be found in less than quadratic time?
